title: 限时写作：流程、地图与阶段测评 · Four listening sections
instructions: 原创模拟训练材料；先独立作答，再核对依据。四节音频共40题，按顺序听音作答。合成训练音频时长不同于正式考试。
transcript:
Section 1: A Community Map-Making Workshop

Mia: Hi, Tom. Thanks for coming to help with the community map project. I heard you’ve been involved in map-making before.
Tom: Yes, I have. I used to work for a small environmental charity, and we made maps of local green spaces. But that was a few years ago, so I’m a bit rusty.
Mia: That’s still useful experience. So, the workshop is next Saturday, right?
Tom: Actually, it’s been moved to Sunday. The community centre had a double booking, so we lost our Saturday slot. The workshop will now be on Sunday, from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m.
Mia: Oh, I didn’t know that. Thanks for telling me. And where is it being held?
Tom: It’s in the small hall at the back of the community centre, not the main hall. The main hall is being used for a children’s party that day.
Mia: Got it. So what exactly will we be doing in the workshop?
Tom: Well, the first part is a training session on how to collect data for maps. We’ll be shown how to use a simple GPS app on our phones to record locations. Then, after lunch, we’ll go out in small groups to map the area around the centre. Each group will be given a different street to cover.
Mia: That sounds good. Will we need to bring anything?
Tom: Yes, you should bring a smartphone if you have one, because the GPS app only works on phones. Also, wear comfortable shoes because we’ll be walking outside for about two hours. Oh, and bring a packed lunch. The café nearby is closed for renovation.
Mia: OK. And is there a fee for the workshop?
Tom: It’s free for volunteers, but there’s a small charge of £5 to cover the cost of materials, like printed maps and clipboards. You can pay on the day, in cash or by card.
Mia: That’s reasonable. How many people have signed up so far?
Tom: We’ve had 18 people register, but the maximum is 20, so there are still a couple of places left. Actually, wait—I think it’s 19 now. One more person signed up this morning.
Mia: OK, so just one place left. And who is leading the workshop?
Tom: The main trainer is Dr. Sarah Chen, who is a geography lecturer at the local university. She’s done a lot of work with community groups. She’ll be assisted by two volunteers from the centre.
Mia: Great. Will we get a certificate or something at the end?
Tom: Yes, everyone who completes the workshop will receive a certificate of participation. It’s not a formal qualification, but it’s nice to have. Also, the maps we produce will be displayed in the community centre library for a month.
Mia: That’s a nice touch. One last thing—is the workshop suitable for beginners? My neighbour might be interested.
Tom: Yes, it’s designed for people with no previous experience. The training session starts with the basics, so beginners are welcome. But they should let us know in advance so we can prepare enough materials.
Mia: I’ll tell her. Thanks, Tom. See you on Sunday.
Tom: See you then. Don’t forget your phone and lunch!

Section 2: City Library Writing Workshop: Procedures, Maps, and Progress Checks

Good morning, everyone. Welcome to the City Library Writing Workshop. My name is Anna, and I am the workshop coordinator. Today I will explain the procedures, show you the map, and describe the progress checks. Please listen carefully because some information has changed since last month.

First, the registration procedure. When you arrive, you should go to the front desk and show your library card. The card is checked by a staff member, and then you receive a blue folder. Inside the folder, you will find a timetable and a map. Please do not write on the map because it is reused every week. If you do not have a library card, you can apply for one at the office on the second floor. The application form is completed online, and the card is usually ready in ten minutes.

Now, let me describe the map. The workshop room is on the first floor, next to the children's reading area. The room is called the Green Room. To get there, enter the main door and walk straight past the information desk. Turn left at the stairs, and the Green Room is the second door on your right. The café is on the ground floor, opposite the main door. The quiet study area is on the second floor, above the office. The toilets are on every floor, near the lifts.

Next, the writing stages. Each session has three stages. In the first stage, you plan your ideas on paper. In the second stage, you write a short draft. In the third stage, you review your draft with a partner. The draft is not collected by the teacher, so you can keep it. However, the review notes are shared with the group at the end of the session. Please bring a pen and paper because computers are not provided in the Green Room.

Finally, the progress checks. There are two checks during the course. The first check is in week three, and the second check is in week six. The checks are marked by two teachers, and you receive a short report. The report is sent to your email address within five days. If you miss a check, you can take it on the following Saturday. The make-up check is held in the Blue Room, not the Green Room. Also, the workshop starts at nine thirty, not nine o'clock as the old timetable says. The old timetable was printed last year, so please ignore the time on it.

One more thing. The library is closed on public holidays, but the workshop still runs online. The online link is sent by email one day before the session. If you have questions, please ask me at the front desk. Thank you for listening.

Section 3: Planning a Timed Writing Task: Process, Map, and Progress Check

Tutor: Good morning, everyone. Today we’re going to talk about your timed writing task on processes and maps. Let’s start with the process diagram you saw last week. Mia, can you remind us what the first stage involves?
Mia: Yes, the first stage is when the raw materials are collected and then they are transported to the factory.
Tutor: Exactly. And what happens after that?
Mia: After that, the materials are weighed and sorted by machine. Then they are mixed with water.
Tutor: Good. Now, Leo, what about the map question? What changes were shown between 1990 and 2020?
Leo: In 1990, there was a small park in the north, but by 2020 it had been replaced by a car park. Also, the river was widened and a new bridge was built across it.
Tutor: Right. So you need to describe the changes using the passive voice, for example, ‘the park was replaced’ and ‘a bridge was built’. Now, let’s think about the structure of your essay. How should you organise the process description?
Mia: We should start with an introduction that says what the process is, then describe the stages in order, using sequencing words like ‘first’, ‘next’, ‘after that’, and finally a conclusion.
Tutor: Yes, and don’t forget to use linking words between sentences, such as ‘however’, ‘therefore’, and ‘in addition’. Now, about the progress check: you will have a short test next week. It will include a process description and a map description. You will have 20 minutes for each part.
Leo: Will we be allowed to use a dictionary?
Tutor: No, dictionaries are not permitted during the test. But you can use a plan. Now, let’s review the passive voice. Mia, can you give me an example from the process?
Mia: The materials are collected.
Tutor: Good. And in the past? Leo?
Leo: The park was replaced by a car park.
Tutor: Perfect. Now, one more thing: when you describe a map, you should use location words like ‘in the north’, ‘to the south of’, ‘next to’, and ‘opposite’. Also, remember to mention the changes in the passive, for example, ‘the river was widened’. Now, let’s talk about the assessment criteria. Your writing will be assessed on task achievement, coherence, vocabulary, and grammar. You need to write at least 150 words for each task. Any questions?
Mia: How many stages are there in the process we saw?
Tutor: There are five stages in total. The first stage is collection, the second is transportation, the third is weighing and sorting, the fourth is mixing, and the fifth is packaging. Now, let’s do a quick practice. I’ll give you a map and you describe the changes. Remember to use the passive and sequencing words. We’ll check your answers together.

Section 4: The Process of Making a Simple Map: A Lecture on Sequence and Passive Voice

Good morning, everyone. Today I’m going to talk about the process of making a simple map, and I’ll also explain how passive voice and sequencing words are used to describe this process. This is a simulated lecture for your listening practice. Please listen carefully and answer the questions as you go.

First, let’s look at the overall stages. A map is usually created in four main stages: planning, data collection, drawing, and checking. These stages are followed in order, and each stage has its own steps. The first stage, planning, involves deciding what the map will show and who will use it. For example, a map for tourists might highlight hotels and restaurants, while a map for hikers might show paths and hills. This decision is made before any drawing begins.

Next, data collection. Information is gathered from various sources, such as satellite images, existing maps, and field surveys. The data is then checked for accuracy. Any errors are corrected at this stage. After the data is collected and checked, it is organized into a database. This database is used later when the map is drawn.

Now, the drawing stage. The map is drawn using special software. First, a base layer is created, which shows the outline of the area. Then, features such as roads, rivers, and buildings are added one by one. Each feature is placed in its correct position according to the data. Labels are added last, so that the map is easy to read. The drawing process is often repeated several times to improve clarity.

Finally, the checking stage. The finished map is reviewed by a team of experts. They look for mistakes and suggest improvements. If any mistakes are found, the map is sent back to the drawing stage. This cycle may be repeated until the map is accurate. Once the map is approved, it is printed or published online.

Now, let’s focus on the language used to describe these processes. Passive voice is common because the focus is on the map, not on the person making it. For example, we say “The map is drawn using software” rather than “Someone draws the map using software.” Sequencing words such as first, then, next, and finally help to show the order of steps. For instance, “First, a base layer is created. Then, features are added.” These words make the process clear and easy to follow.

Let me give you an example of a complete description: “First, the area is planned. Next, data is collected and checked. Then, the map is drawn, and features are added. Finally, the map is reviewed and published.” Notice how passive voice and sequencing words work together.

To sum up, making a simple map involves four stages, and each stage is completed in order. Passive voice and sequencing words are used to describe the process clearly. I hope this lecture helps you understand both the process and the language. Thank you.

grammar.title: 被动语态、顺序、地点、变化及句子间衔接
grammar.explanation: 英语中常用被动语态（be + 过去分词）来强调动作的承受者或当执行者不重要时。顺序词（first, then, after that）帮助组织信息。地点表达常用介词短语（in, at, on）。变化可以用动词如move, change, become等。句子间衔接可用连接词如but, so, because等。
grammar.example: The workshop will now be on Sunday, from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m.
